title: Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities
content:
### 2.2 Suitability and quality of the measures to maximise expected outcomes and impacts, as set out in the dissemination and exploitation plan, including communication activities

#### 2.2.1 The governance architecture of dissemination and exploitation: WP5 and its two foundational deliverables

The project's dissemination and exploitation activities are governed by two contractual deliverables under WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), each due at month 6 — before any primary research deliverable is produced from WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), or WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration). The Data Management Plan (D5-01, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) are the formal governance instruments through which the project's open-science commitments become binding and its dissemination strategy is confirmed before any of the outputs it must govern are generated.

The governance significance of the month 6 timing is not administrative convenience. A FAIR compliance framework adopted after data collection begins can describe what was done but cannot shape how it was done. D5-01 at month 6 places the FAIR governance commitment — covering findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability — before the WP1 Earth observation data acquisition and harmonisation, before the WP3 field measurement campaigns at Hungarian tomato farm sites accessed through AgroVIR, and before the WP2 probabilistic model code development that will be released as open-source software. This sequencing ensures that D5-01 governs the data formats, metadata standards, and repository choices that are made during the research work — not retrospectively applied to data collected and stored in a format inconsistent with FAIR principles. Similarly, D5-02 at month 6 confirms open-access dissemination routes for all primary outputs of WP1, WP2, and WP3 before the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14), the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20), and the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24) are produced. Each primary deliverable is released under a pre-specified, confirmed open-access route rather than arranged ad hoc at each release point — a structural guarantee of dissemination quality that ad hoc planning cannot provide.

The Data Management Plan (D5-01) governs three structurally distinct data asset classes that present different FAIR challenges. The multi-sensor Earth observation datasets of WP1 — harmonising Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, secured PlanetScope imagery (RQ8), and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis — present the interoperability challenge of combining sources with different spatial resolutions, temporal baselines, and data formats into a standardised, openly described representation that the precision agriculture and Earth observation communities can access and reuse without proprietary dependencies. The interoperability dimension of FAIR is particularly consequential here, because the project's methodological contribution rests on the harmonisation of heterogeneous EO sources: an open release that does not document the harmonisation protocol in a machine-readable, interoperable form fails to transmit the most technically challenging aspect of the contribution. The probabilistic model code of WP1 and WP2 — the Route A (direct probabilistic fusion) and Route B (homogeneous-patch proxy, RQ2) diagnostic implementations and the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and counterfactual simulation code — presents the reusability challenge of ensuring that software is licensed, documented, and deposited in a form that enables independent replication. The Hungarian tomato field validation dataset of WP3 — comprising the non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurements of chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance (RQ4), the uncertainty-calibration evidence against the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5), and the co-located seasonal campaign measurements from the Route B covariation test (RQ9) — presents the findability challenge of making a site-specific field dataset persistently discoverable and citable. D5-01 is the instrument through which each of these asset-class-specific FAIR requirements is addressed prospectively rather than retrofitted.

The Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02) is the operative instrument for international scientific visibility and institutional reputation. By confirming open-access routes for WP1–WP3 primary outputs at month 6, D5-02 ensures that the project's subsequent releases are aligned with the journals, repositories, and community channels that the target scientific audiences actually consult. D5-02 is thus the key governance instrument for EI-04 (Increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation(s) and, by extension, of the European Research Area): international scientific visibility requires channel-appropriate, audience-informed dissemination, and D5-02 is where that strategy is confirmed in contractually binding form before any output requires it. Both D5-01 and D5-02 are led by Dr. Rositsa Cholakova as WP5 lead, establishing the fellow's direct accountability for the project's open-science governance from the first months of the action and embedding open-science competence development within the WP5 research responsibility rather than treating it as an external administrative obligation.

#### 2.2.2 Scientific dissemination: target groups, dissemination channels, and temporal phasing

The primary scientific dissemination output is the body of peer-reviewed open-access publications arising from WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), and WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), constituting project outcome OUT-5 (Peer-reviewed publications and open science outputs). These publications are the primary channel through which the project's core scientific novelty — the end-to-end probabilistic coupling of multi-sensor Earth observation with uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and water-use-efficiency-oriented irrigation decision recommendation (RQ6) — is submitted to peer review and made available to the scientific communities capable of evaluating, replicating, and building upon it.

The target audience for the primary scientific publications is defined with precision by the project's research position. The project addresses the intersection of three active scientific communities. The remote sensing and Earth observation community is addressed through the multi-sensor fusion methodology and probabilistic field-state estimation results constituting project outcome OUT-1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor field-state diagnosis method): the specific novelty is the probabilistic coupling of Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, secured PlanetScope imagery (RQ8), and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis to produce posterior estimates of root-zone soil moisture and crop water status (RQ3) with explicit, honest uncertainty. The precision agriculture and crop modelling community is addressed through project outcome OUT-2 (Uncertainty-aware AquaCrop decision engine): the specific novelty is the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration retaining an honest parameter posterior, coupled with counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles and WUE-based decision recommendation (RQ6). The crop physiology and field sensing community is addressed through project outcome OUT-3 (Field-validation dataset and uncertainty-calibration evidence): the specific novelty is the probabilistic validation framework grounded in non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurement (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance, RQ4) and assessed against the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5). Addressing all three communities through a single end-to-end probabilistic pipeline — from observation through diagnosis through decision — is the project's primary novelty claim, and each publication sub-set addresses the specific disciplinary sub-community most capable of evaluating the contribution that sub-set makes.

All publications are made available under open-access routes in compliance with the Horizon Europe open-access mandate, with routes confirmed by D5-02 at month 6. Publication phasing is aligned with the sequential completion of the primary research work packages: publications from WP1 diagnostic modelling are prepared following D1-01 (Diagnostic model specification and calibration report, month 14); publications from WP2 decision engine and demonstrator work follow D2-01 (Decision engine and demonstrator software, month 20); and publications from WP3 field validation follow D3-01 (Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report, month 24). This sequencing ensures that publications are grounded in completed, validated research. The uncertainty-calibration criterion (RQ5: 90% prediction intervals containing the truth approximately 90% of the time) and the pilot-success criterion (RQ7: the RQ5 calibration target met on the validation set) serve as the project's scientifically self-imposed threshold for publication readiness: results are submitted for peer review when the validation evidence is available, not before. This approach connects the scientific dissemination strategy directly to the project's methodological commitment to honest uncertainty reporting — a connection that is independently verifiable by comparing the calibration evidence in D3-01 with the claims made in the WP3 publication.

Beyond peer-reviewed publications, international conference presentations constitute a second scientific dissemination channel targeting the same primary audiences. Conference venues including ISPRS and IEEE IGARSS host the remote sensing and Earth observation communities that constitute the project's primary scientific peer group. Conference dissemination is timed following D1-01 (month 14) and progresses through WP2 and WP3 completion. Conference participation serves EI-02 (Increased and broadened research and innovation impact through enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers and the general public) through the specific mechanism of scientific network building: conference presentation creates opportunities for community-level feedback, collaboration, and exposure of the project's probabilistic multi-sensor framework before journal publication, accelerating the circulation of methodological contributions within the communities best positioned to extend them. The scientific communication competence required to execute this dissemination strategy is formally addressed in the Career Development Plan (D4-01, WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge, month 3), which includes scientific communication as a named training dimension within the mandatory MSCA-PF transferable-skills curriculum, ensuring that the fellow is explicitly trained in communicating with scientific peers and the general public as a formal, auditable project commitment from action start.

#### 2.2.3 Open science outputs as the project's most durable dissemination infrastructure: FAIR data and software releases

The project's open science outputs are its most durable dissemination mechanism, because unlike conference presentations — whose reach is bounded in time and space — FAIR-released code, software, and datasets remain accessible, citable, and reusable indefinitely by the global scientific community, enabling a self-sustaining dissemination dynamic that persists without further investment from the project team. Three primary open science output releases are produced at defined points during the fellowship, each governed by D5-01 and confirmed in D5-02.

**WP1 probabilistic diagnosis code released alongside the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, month 14, WP1: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state).** The open-source release of the WP1 probabilistic fusion code makes the project's Route A and Route B (RQ2: homogeneous-patch proxy) diagnostic implementations available to the remote sensing and precision agriculture communities for inspection, replication, and extension. The primary target audience for this release comprises geoinformatics researchers and data scientists working on multi-sensor crop-water-state estimation, for whom a FAIR-compliant, openly licensed implementation of a probabilistic pipeline fusing Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope, and ERA5 reanalysis inputs for tomato water-stress diagnosis provides a reproducible computational foundation not currently available as open infrastructure. The interoperability dimension of FAIR is particularly consequential for this release: the project's methodological contribution rests on the harmonisation of heterogeneous EO sources with different spatial resolutions, temporal baselines, and data formats, and an open release that does not document the harmonisation protocol in machine-readable, interoperable form would fail to transmit the technically most significant aspect of the contribution to the community that needs to evaluate and extend it.

**The Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20, WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) released as an open-source artefact.** D2-01 is the project's primary open science output because it is the only publicly available end-to-end implementation of the full pipeline — from multi-sensor observation through probabilistic crop-water-state diagnosis through uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and counterfactual simulation to WUE-optimised irrigation recommendation (RQ6). Its open release makes this pipeline available not only for scientific scrutiny but for adaptation and further TRL progression by agri-tech developers and future research groups in other crop and geography contexts beyond the tomato horticulture context of this project. The target audience for D2-01's open release extends the WP1 code audience to include crop modelling research groups interested in uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration, agronomists assessing the decision-support architecture, and practice-facing agri-tech developers for whom the demonstrator's user-interface design and decision-output format are directly relevant for adaptation. AgroVIR's farmer-facing assessment of D2-01's WUE recommendations during WP3 field validation constitutes an initial real-world uptake signal at TRL 3-4 (RQ10) — the appropriate form of exploitation for a research prototype at this stage of development.

**The Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24, WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) released under FAIR principles with a dataset DOI or open repository reference.** D3-01 is released as a dataset assigned a DOI or open repository reference, making it persistently findable and citable in compliance with the findability and accessibility dimensions of FAIR. The field validation dataset — comprising the multi-sensor EO input stack, the non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurements (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance, RQ4) from Hungarian tomato farms accessed via AgroVIR, the uncertainty-calibration evidence from the prediction-interval coverage assessment (RQ5), and the co-located seasonal campaign measurements from the Route B covariation test (RQ9) — constitutes an independent scientific contribution beyond the diagnostic and decision-engine methodology it validates. A FAIR-released, openly accessible validation benchmark from Hungarian tomato field sites provides the precision agriculture sensing community with a dataset for calibrating and comparing probabilistic field-state estimation methods regardless of whether those methods use the specific D1-01 or D2-01 pipeline. The reusability of D3-01 is therefore broader than the project's own use case, extending the dataset's dissemination impact to any research group working on plant-stress remote sensing or crop-water diagnostics.

The three-release timeline — code at month 14, software and demonstrator at month 20, dataset at month 24 — is coordinated under D5-01's single FAIR compliance framework, ensuring that the three releases form a coherent, interoperable open research infrastructure rather than three independent artefacts. The dataset DOI assigned to D3-01 and the open repositories for D1-01 code and D2-01 software provide persistent access points that accumulate citations over time, creating a self-reinforcing dissemination mechanism that extends the project's impact well beyond the fellowship period without requiring continued investment from the project team.

#### 2.2.4 Communication to non-specialist target audiences: AgroVIR and curriculum integration

The project's scientific dissemination reaches the research communities positioned to evaluate and extend the technical methods. Its communication activities reach two non-specialist audiences through two distinct and complementary channels, each designed to be substantive rather than cosmetic.

**AgroVIR as the channel to Hungarian tomato farmers and the horticultural sector.** AgroVIR (Hungary), the project's non-academic associated partner, provides farmer access and field-validation site logistics for WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration). This operational context creates an organic communication channel to non-specialist audiences: the WP3 field validation protocol is conducted at Hungarian tomato farm sites that AgroVIR makes accessible, and the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20) is presented to and assessed by agricultural users in this same context. Communication to the agricultural sector is embedded in the scientific validation process rather than appended to it as a separate outreach activity. Farmers and agricultural sector actors engaged through AgroVIR encounter the project's WUE-optimised irrigation recommendations through direct exposure to the TRL 3-4 demonstrator's decision outputs — a form of communication that is immediate, contextually grounded, and practice-facing in a way that a brochure or press release cannot be.

The significance of this communication channel extends beyond its immediate reach to the specific farms engaged. AgroVIR's farmers assess the demonstrator's outputs against their own farming experience and operational decision-making context, generating feedback that informs both the project's scientific assessment of the demonstrator's TRL 3-4 operational credibility and the agricultural sector's exposure to the concept of uncertainty-aware remote-sensing-driven irrigation decision support. This creates a two-directional knowledge exchange: the project communicates results to the agricultural sector; the agricultural sector communicates practice-facing requirements back to the research — an exchange that directly realises EI-07 (New mind-sets and approaches to R&I work fostered through international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary experience, enriching the broader European research culture) and constitutes the inter-sectoral knowledge flow that MSCA-PF inter-sectoral engagement is designed to produce. AgroVIR does not own or operate any project output and its role is bounded to farmer access and field-validation logistics — a scope proportionate to the project's single-researcher scale and consistent with the confirmed associated-partner arrangement. It does not represent a commitment to operational deployment or commercial transfer that would be premature at TRL 3-4 (RQ10).

**Curriculum integration at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest as the channel to the next generation of geoinformatics and remote sensing researchers.** Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest hosts active geoinformatics, remote sensing, and precision agriculture MSc and PhD programmes within its Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics. The project's open-source code (released with D1-01 at month 14 and as D2-01 at month 20) and FAIR-released dataset (D3-01 at month 24) represent teachable, integrable research outputs: concrete implementations of Bayesian multi-sensor fusion, uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration, and WUE-oriented decision support that students and academic staff can examine, reproduce, and build upon within a course or research project context. Curriculum integration is timed following D1-01 (month 14) and D2-01 (month 20) delivery, with the integration pathway confirmed FAIR-compliant under D5-01 (month 6) well before D1-01 is delivered — ensuring that the open licence terms and data format choices governing D1-01 and D2-01 are set with curriculum integration in mind from the start of the research work.

The durability of this communication channel distinguishes it structurally from time-bounded communication events. A module or teaching dataset integrated into a recurring academic course reaches new cohorts of MSc and PhD students in every academic year following integration — compounding the communication impact beyond the fellowship period without requiring continued effort from the project team. This is the mechanism through which curriculum integration realises EI-06 (Regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations, sustaining knowledge circulation between research and education): the word "regular" in EI-06 requires a recurrent, self-sustaining feedback mechanism, which curriculum integration at a teaching university provides, rather than a single communication event. The project's specific outputs — the probabilistic field-state diagnosis method (OUT-1: Probabilistic multi-sensor field-state diagnosis method) and the open-source end-to-end pipeline (D1-01 code, D2-01 software) — represent novel, open, peer-reviewable contributions to Bayesian multi-sensor fusion and uncertainty-aware decision support that advance the state of geoinformatics and precision agriculture teaching, rather than merely illustrating what is already standard practice. The open licensing and FAIR compliance of the research outputs are the enabling conditions for this sustainable integration: they ensure that ELTE's academic staff can incorporate and maintain the teaching materials without proprietary barriers and independently of the fellow's continued physical presence.

#### 2.2.5 Exploitation strategy: the open-infrastructure pathway at TRL 3-4

The project's confirmed TRL target — research prototype at TRL 3-4 (RQ10) — defines both the boundaries within which the exploitation strategy must operate and the form of exploitation that is appropriate and proportionate to a 24-month single-researcher European Fellowship. At TRL 3-4, the project has produced a validated research prototype with demonstrated calibration evidence; it has not produced a market-ready product with verified operational performance at scale. The exploitation strategy must therefore be designed to extract maximum value from what a TRL 3-4 prototype actually is — a reproducible, scientifically validated foundation for further development — rather than from what it is not.

The Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, month 20, WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) is the project's primary exploitation vehicle, because it is the concrete, openly licensed artefact through which the project's full end-to-end pipeline — from multi-sensor observation through probabilistic crop-water-state estimation through WUE-optimised irrigation recommendation — is made available to the global precision agriculture and crop modelling research community for replication, adaptation, and further TRL progression. Its open release makes the specific end-to-end pipeline available to research groups and agri-tech developers with greater resources and longer timelines than a 24-month fellowship, enabling further development toward higher TRL without the restriction of commercial licensing arrangements that would slow adoption. AgroVIR's farmer-facing assessment of D2-01's WUE recommendations during WP3 field validation constitutes a TRL 3-4 uptake signal: it demonstrates operational exposure in a real agricultural context and documents the practice-facing feedback that future higher-TRL development requires.

Post-fellowship sustainability of the exploitation pathway is secured through three complementary mechanisms grounded in the confirmed project architecture. First, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest retains the validated probabilistic fusion methodology, code (D1-01: Diagnostic model specification and calibration report accompanying code, and D2-01: Decision engine and demonstrator software), and benchmark dataset (D3-01: Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report) as open research infrastructure within its Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics. This infrastructure is integrated into the ongoing research programme of the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29), led by Dr. András Jung, providing the group context in which the probabilistic fusion methodology can be applied to new crop species, geographic contexts, and sensor configurations in follow-on research. Dr. Jung's co-founding of Cubert GmbH and Brightic Research demonstrates a personal track record of translating remote-sensing research instrumentation from laboratory to commercial deployment — the knowledge valorisation pathway through which TRL 3-4 prototypes progress toward operational products — and provides the mentorship environment in which the project's open prototype can be developed further by the group beyond the fellowship period. Second, the global FAIR release of all primary code and data assets under D5-01 ensures that the international research community can build on, extend, and cite the project's results independently without access barriers, sustaining scientific impact without dependence on the project's continued funding. The dataset DOI assigned to D3-01 and the open repositories for D1-01 code and D2-01 software provide persistent, citable access points that accumulate citations and enable independent replication over time, creating a self-reinforcing dissemination mechanism. Third, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's post-fellowship cross-disciplinary career profile — coupling plant physiology and non-destructive stress phenotyping with geoinformatics and remote sensing, documented in the Career Development Plan (D4-01, WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge, month 3) and evidenced by the FAIR-released, peer-reviewed deliverables D1-01, D2-01, and D3-01 — enables continued engagement with both the precision agriculture and Earth observation research communities, sustaining the fellow's contribution to the adoption and extension of the project's methods beyond the fellowship period.

#### 2.2.6 Intellectual property management strategy

The project's intellectual property management strategy is defined by a single, coherent decision: no patent protection is sought for any primary research output. This decision is grounded in three converging rationales, each project-specific rather than generic.

The first rationale is the confirmed TRL target. The project operates at TRL 3-4 (RQ10): a research prototype demonstrating the principle and validating the methodology. Patent protection is an appropriate IP mechanism when a specific, commercially deployable embodiment of an invention needs to be protected against competitive copying. At TRL 3-4, the project's outputs are methods, code, and validation data — the scientific substrate from which higher-TRL development might proceed in the hands of the research and development community, not proprietary technical implementations that a specific commercial actor has invested in bringing to market. Patent protection at TRL 3-4 would impose a restriction on the scientific community's ability to replicate, scrutinise, and build upon the methods without adding the commercial value that patent protection is designed to protect.

The second rationale is the project's methodological commitment to honest uncertainty propagation. The 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) is the project's adopted definition of honest uncertainty — the requirement that model outputs report what they do not know with the same rigour as what they know. This commitment is inseparable from the open scientific scrutiny that peer review and open-source release provide: independent replication of the calibration evidence is the mechanism through which the honesty of the uncertainty claim can be verified. A patent protection strategy restricting access to the diagnostic pipeline would prevent independent replication of the calibration evidence, undermining the scientific foundation of the uncertainty claim. Open-source release and open data release are not merely compliance with the Horizon Europe open-science mandate; they are the conditions under which the project's central methodological commitment — honest uncertainty propagation from observation to decision — is scientifically defensible.

The third rationale is alignment with the MSCA-PF instrument's knowledge transfer and ERA capacity building objectives. Patent protection restricts knowledge transfer to the licensor's terms, limiting the ability of other research groups to use and extend the methodology freely. Open licensing removes that restriction, enabling maximum transfer of the project's methods to the global scientific community, directly realising EI-03 (Stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations and better transfer of knowledge between participating organisations), and maximising Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest's international visibility as the institution that produced and openly released the end-to-end pipeline, directly realising EI-04 (Increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation(s) and, by extension, of the European Research Area). The choice of permissive open-source licensing for all software outputs — D1-01 code and D2-01 software — and FAIR data release for D3-01 is therefore simultaneously an open-science compliance measure and a strategic knowledge-transfer decision consistent with the project's contribution to ERA research capacity.

The prospective IP governance instrument is D5-01 (Data Management Plan, month 6, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), which specifies open licence terms for each primary output before those outputs are produced, ensuring that open licensing decisions are made in advance rather than negotiated at the point of release when third-party IP complications could complicate the commitment. The Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) confirms the open-access routes and dissemination channels under which the licensed outputs are published. Together, D5-01 and D5-02 constitute the project's complete IP management and dissemination governance framework, established at month 6 as binding commitments applicable to all subsequent output releases.

#### 2.2.7 Proportionality, phased concrete actions during and after the project, and mapping to EI-02, EI-03, EI-04, and EI-06

**Proportionality.** The dissemination and exploitation measures described in the preceding sub-sections are proportionate to the scale and character of a 24-month, single-researcher European Fellowship producing a research prototype at TRL 3-4. The plan does not assert measures appropriate to a large-consortium Research and Innovation Action with multiple commercial partners and a near-market prototype. It is calibrated to what this fellowship can genuinely deliver with quality: open-access publications validated against the RQ5/RQ7 calibration evidence before submission, FAIR data and code releases with documentation sufficient for independent replication, AgroVIR-mediated communication to the agricultural sector integrated into the scientific field validation, curriculum integration at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest drawing on openly licensed research outputs, and an open-infrastructure exploitation pathway appropriate to TRL 3-4 (RQ10). Each measure is proportionate, bounded by confirmed project activities, and linked to named contractual deliverables with confirmed due months.

**Phased concrete actions during and after the project:**

At month 3, the Career Development Plan (D4-01, WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) is submitted. D4-01 includes scientific communication as a named mandatory training dimension within the MSCA-PF transferable-skills framework, establishing the fellow's training in communicating with scientific peers and non-specialist audiences as a formal, auditable commitment at action start — before the primary research outputs requiring dissemination have been produced.

At month 6, both the Data Management Plan (D5-01, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) and the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) are submitted, establishing the FAIR compliance framework for all primary WP1–WP3 data assets and confirming open-access routes for all primary WP1–WP3 outputs. This simultaneous month 6 milestone creates the project's complete open-science governance architecture as a single coherent governance event, placing the full FAIR framework (D5-01) and dissemination strategy (D5-02) on record before any primary data collection begins in earnest.

At month 14, the Diagnostic model specification and calibration report (D1-01, WP1: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) is delivered, accompanied by the open-source release of the Route A and Route B probabilistic diagnosis code in an open repository under D5-01's FAIR framework. Primary WP1 peer-reviewed publication is in preparation, targeting open-access venues confirmed in D5-02. International conference presentation on WP1 results at venues including ISPRS and IEEE IGARSS is submitted following D1-01 delivery. Curriculum integration at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest of D1-01 and the accompanying open code begins.

At month 20, the Decision engine and demonstrator software (D2-01, WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) is delivered and released as an open-source artefact in a confirmed open repository under D5-01's FAIR framework. AgroVIR-mediated farmer assessment of D2-01's WUE recommendations from WP3 Hungarian tomato field validation sites provides a TRL 3-4 uptake signal and communicates the project's results to the horticultural sector. WP2 peer-reviewed publication targeting the uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration and counterfactual simulation methodology is in preparation. Curriculum integration of D2-01 at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest continues.

At month 24, the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) is delivered and released under FAIR principles with a dataset DOI or open repository reference. WP3 peer-reviewed publication incorporating the Route B covariation validation evidence (RQ9) and the uncertainty-calibration evidence (RQ5, RQ7) is in submission or final preparation. The project's complete open research infrastructure is in place: three FAIR-released open science outputs covering the full end-to-end pipeline from EO observation to WUE-optimised irrigation recommendation, all reachable through persistent, citable references confirmed in D5-02.

Post-fellowship, open-access publications from WP1–WP3 research are published in venues confirmed in D5-02. The FAIR-released open outputs — D1-01 code, D2-01 software, D3-01 dataset — continue to be citable and reusable by the global community, accumulating citations and enabling independent extension of the methodology in other crop, geography, and sensor contexts. Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest retains the open research infrastructure for continued use in research and teaching within the Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics and the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29). Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's cross-disciplinary career profile enables continued engagement with the precision agriculture and Earth observation communities, sustaining the fellow's contribution to the adoption and extension of the project's methods beyond the fellowship.

**Contribution to EI-02.** EI-02 (Increased and broadened research and innovation impact through enhanced networking and communication capacities with scientific peers and the general public) is realised through the combination of: OUT-5 (Peer-reviewed publications and open science outputs) — the peer-reviewed open-access publications from WP1–WP3 constituting the substantive R&I content the fellow's communication activities disseminate; WP4's training of the fellow in scientific communication (D4-01, month 3) as a named mandatory dimension; AgroVIR-mediated communication to the agricultural sector integrated within WP3 field validation; and curriculum integration at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest of open-source outputs confirmed FAIR-compliant by D5-01 (month 6) and D5-02 (month 6). The communication and networking capacity dimension of EI-02 is served both by the formal communication training in D4-01 and by the substantive quality of the outputs being communicated: the precision of the probabilistic novelty claim, validated against the RQ5/RQ7 calibration criteria, provides the scientific content that makes the networking and citation impact of EI-02 credible.

**Contribution to EI-03.** EI-03 (Stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations and better transfer of knowledge between participating organisations) is realised through the durable addition of the project's validated open-source methodology (D1-01 code, D2-01 software) and benchmark dataset (D3-01) to Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest's research infrastructure in remote sensing, probabilistic machine learning, and precision agriculture decision support, strengthening ELTE's R&I output in areas the project's activities have established as new competences of the institution. The two-way knowledge transfer formally structured in WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge) and documented in D4-01 (Career Development Plan, month 3) — contributing Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's plant-physiology and non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise to ELTE's geoinformatics group, and transferring ELTE's geoinformatics and hyperspectral-fusion methods to the fellow — constitutes the knowledge transfer between participating organisations that EI-03 requires, producing R&I capacity at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest that neither the fellow nor the host group could have generated independently.

**Contribution to EI-04.** EI-04 (Increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation(s) and, by extension, of the European Research Area) is realised through the Dissemination and exploitation plan (D5-02, month 6) establishing internationally positioned open-access dissemination pathways for all WP1–WP3 primary outputs, and through the Field validation dataset and uncertainty calibration report (D3-01, month 24) released as a FAIR benchmark dataset from Hungarian tomato field sites — providing an internationally citable, reproducible contribution that addresses the identified empty cell of the reviewed gap matrix (real-time decision support combined with PlanetScope high-resolution imagery). Open-access publication of results addressing a specific, reviewable literature gap increases Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest's international citation footprint and reputation in multi-sensor Earth observation and uncertainty-quantification research communities, enhancing ELTE's attractiveness as a fellowship host and research partner within the European Research Area.

**Contribution to EI-06.** EI-06 (Regular feedback of research results into teaching and education at participating organisations, sustaining knowledge circulation between research and education) is realised through the curriculum integration at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest of the open-source code (D1-01, D2-01) and FAIR-released dataset (D3-01), confirmed FAIR-compliant under D5-01 (month 6), timed from month 14 and continuing through month 24 and post-fellowship. The open licensing and FAIR compliance of the research outputs are the enabling conditions for sustainable curriculum integration: they ensure that ELTE's academic staff can incorporate and maintain the teaching materials without proprietary barriers and independently of the fellow's continued involvement, creating the recurrent, self-sustaining research-to-education feedback cycle that the word "regular" in EI-06 specifies.
